Rainilaiarivony: Prime Minister of Madagascar from 1864 to 1895.
Before circling the Moon 45 times as command module pilot on Apollo 12, this naval aviator had already flown in space piloting Gemini 11 — which astronaut?
Richard F. Gordon Jr.: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1929–2017)
Appointed Deputy to the Führer, this Nazi leader stunned everyone by flying solo to Scotland in 1941 to try to negotiate Britain out of the war — who was he?

This Indian Army major with the National Security Guard's elite commando unit was killed in action during the 2008 Mumbai attacks and posthumously received India's highest peacetime gallantry award — who was he?

Once a member of the State Duma, this Russian financial fraudster's donation-based scheme defrauded thousands of investors — and he later claimed the same scheme was behind a bitcoin price rally — who is he?
Ending on the Fourth of July, 1863, this brutal Mississippi River campaign saw Grant trap Pemberton's Confederates in a fortress city — completing the Anaconda Plan's grip on the river. What was it?
Siege of Vicksburg: Battle of the American Civil War.
Son of a Greek Catholic priest in Galicia, he led a radical faction of Ukrainian nationalists and orchestrated the 1934 assassination of a Polish interior minister — who was he?
A former brigadier-general who rose to Speaker of Singapore's Parliament, this politician resigned in 2023 after admitting to a years-long affair with a fellow MP — who is he?
Tan Chuan-Jin: Singaporean politician. Tan Chuan-Jin (born 10 January 1969) is a Singaporean former politician and brigadier-general.
Brother of King Henry VIII's third wife, this nobleman married the king's widow Catherine Parr in 1547 while sparring with his own brother for influence over the young King Edward VI — who was he?
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley: English nobleman (1508–1548)
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
This Indian politician served as Maharashtra's 19th chief minister from 2019 to 2022 while also editing a newspaper for over a decade — who is he?
Uddhav Thackeray: 19th Chief Minister of Maharashtra from 2019 to 2022 (born 1960)
In 1976, this Soviet pilot defected to the West by flying his MiG-25 'Foxbat' jet interceptor to Japan, handing the CIA what George H. W. Bush called an 'intelligence bonanza' — who is he?
Viktor Belenko: Soviet pilot who defected to the West (1947–2023)

Beginning with the 1916 death of Yuan Shikai, this chaotic decade-plus in Chinese history saw the country splinter under rival military cliques until Sun Yat-sen's Nationalists challenged the Beijing government for legitimacy — which period?
Warlord Era: Period in the history of the Republic of China (1916–1928)

Convinced that Protestants and the Catholic majority had to make common cause against the Crown, this revolutionary helped found the Society of United Irishmen in 1791 and became an icon of Irish republicanism — who was he?
A career Army general who became a national hero in the Mexican-American War, this 12th U.S. president died of a stomach illness just 16 months into office — who is he?
Zachary Taylor: President of the United States from 1849 to 1850.
Who among these was born first?
Stephen Hales (born 1677) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was born earliest?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
MUMPS (founded 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Margaret Burbidge is an astronomer. Eleanor Margaret Burbidge, (née Peachey; 12 August 1919 – 5 April 2020) was a British-American observational astronomer and astrophysicist.
Who among these is a mathematician?
D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson is a mathematician. Sir D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson CB FRS FRSE (2 May 1860 – 21 June 1948) was a Scottish biologist, classicist and mathematician.
What is the atomic number of Ununennium?
Ununennium, also known as eka-francium or element 119, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Uue and atomic number 119.
What is the atomic number of Germanium?
Germanium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ge and atomic number 32.
In what year was Ilya Sutskever born?
Ilya Sutskever (Hebrew: איליה סוצקבר; born 1986) is a computer scientist who specializes in machine learning.
In what year was Yulia Tymoshenko born?
Yulia Tymoshenko: Tymoshenko is the leader of the Batkivshchyna (Ukrainian: Батьківщина) political party.
In what year was James Clerk Maxwell born?
James Clerk Maxwell: Maxwell's equations for electromagnetism achieved the second great unification in physics, where the first one had been realised by Isaac Newton.
In what year did Friedrich Engels die?
Friedrich Engels: After Marx's death, Engels served as the editor of his works, completing the second and third volumes of Das Kapital.
In what year did Nikola Tesla die?
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor.
In what year was Carbon discovered?
Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
Which company manufactures Boeing AH-64 Apache?
Boeing AH-64 Apache: Hughes Helicopters. The Apache began as the Model 77 developed by Hughes Helicopters for the United States Army's Advanced Attack Helicopter program to replace the AH-1 Cobra.
Which country is Mikoyan MiG-31 from?
Mikoyan MiG-31: Soviet Union. The MiG-31 is the fastest known operational combat aircraft, with a top speed around 3,000 km/h (1,600 knots).
Who is credited with discovering Hydrus?
Hydrus: Petrus Plancius. Hydrus is a small constellation in the deep southern sky.
Who is credited with discovering Tiktaalik?
Tiktaalik: Neil H. Shubin. Tiktaalik is estimated to have had a total length of 1.25–2.75 metres (4.1–9.0 ft) on the basis of various specimens.
Who is credited with discovering Fluoxetine?
Fluoxetine: David T. Wong. It is also approved for treatment of major depressive disorder in adolescents and children 8 years of age and over.
Who is credited with discovering HTML?
HTML: Tim Berners-Lee. Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) is the standard markup language for documents designed to be displayed in a web browser.
A broad-spectrum benzimidazole drug, this medicine clears intestinal parasites from pinworm to hookworm to tapeworm — which agent is it?
Albendazole is a broad-spectrum antihelmintic and antiprotozoal agent of the benzimidazole type.
Famed for foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry, this French mathematician was also a principal founder of the secretive Bourbaki group — who was he?
André Weil (6 May 1906 - 6 August 1998) was a French mathematician, known for his foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry.
This mid-sized zodiac constellation, sitting between Pisces and Taurus, has represented a ram since late Babylonian times — though its stars once formed a farmhand. Which one is it?
Aries (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac. It is located in the Northern celestial hemisphere between Pisces to the west and Taurus to the east.

Developed in Great Britain around the 1830s from breeds like the Talbot Hound, this scent hound — smaller than the similar-looking foxhound — was originally bred to hunt rabbits and hares — name the breed?
Beagle is a British breed of scent hound, similar in appearance to the much larger foxhound.
A child prodigy who wrote a treatise on conic sections at 16, which Frenchman later traded letters with Fermat on probability and built early calculating machines?
Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 - 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
This small leafy vegetable, a cultivar of cabbage grown for its edible buds, shares its name with a European capital — what is it?
Brussels sprout is a member of the Gemmifera cultivar group of cabbages (Brassica oleracea), grown for its edible buds.

Honored twice by the American Psychological Association — in 1956 for scientific contributions and 1972 for professional ones — this psychologist championed a person-centered approach to therapy — who is he?
Carl Rogers (January 8, 1902 - February 4, 1987) was an American psychologist who was one of the founders of humanistic psychology and was known especially for his person-centered psychotherapy.

This compound is a yellowish-green gas above 11°C, a reddish-brown liquid when cooler, and bright orange crystals when very cold — usually handled in solution as a bleach and disinfectant. What is it?

Chlorine dioxide is a chemical compound with the formula ClO2 that exists as yellowish-green gas above 11 C (52 F), a reddish-brown liquid between 11 and 59 C (52 and 74 F), and as bright orange crystals below 59 C (74 F).
What's the scientific family name for the group of birds that includes both doves and pigeons — stout-bodied birds with small heads and no formal distinction between the two common names?
Columbidae is a bird family consisting of doves and pigeons.
Mostly aquatic mandibulate arthropods, this group spans shrimp, crayfish, copepods, and barnacles — and modern science now files insects in alongside them — what are they?
Crustacean (from Latin word "crustacea" meaning: "those with shells" or "crusted ones") are mandibulate arthropods that are traditionally a part of the paraphyletic subphylum Crustacea.
A colorless organosulfur compound known as the most widely used commercial sulfoxide, an important polar solvent. It leaves a distinctive taste when absorbed through the skin. What is it?
Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) is an organosulfur compound with the formula (CH3)2S=O.

Distinguished by permanently erect front fangs and a habit of rearing up while flaring a neck flap, which family of mostly venomous snakes ranges from an 18 cm white-lipped species to a nearly 6-metre giant?
Elapidae (commonly known as elapids, from Ancient) is a family of snakes characterized by their permanently erect fangs at the front of the mouth.

This simple hydrocarbon gas, the simplest member of a class called alkenes, is the most-produced organic compound on Earth by tonnage, and is the primary building block of a common plastic — what is it?
Ethylene (IUPAC name: ethene) is a hydrocarbon which has the formula C2H4 or H2C=CH2.

Also known as Lasègue–Falret syndrome after the pair of psychiatrists who first described it, this shared delusional disorder is named for the small number of people who typically experience it together — what is it called?

Folie à deux (French for 'madness of two'), also called shared psychosis or shared delusional disorder (SDD), is a rare psychiatric syndrome in which symptoms of a delusional belief are "transmitted" from one individual to another.

A Belgian-British emigrant to New York, this inventor struck gold during a 1906 stay in Central America by perfecting an early instant-coffee process and building a company to mass-produce it — who was he?
George Washington (inventor) (May 20, 1871 - March 29, 1946) was a Belgian-British inventor and businessman.

This small, hardy aquarium fish native to northeast South America gives birth to live young rather than laying eggs, and now ranks among the world's most widely kept tropical species — what fish is it?
Guppy (Poecilia reticulata), also known as the millionfish or rainbow fish, is a member of the family Poeciliidae and, akin to most New World members of the family, is classified as a livebearer.
This field studies the methods historians use — their sources, techniques, and theoretical approaches — in turning the past into an academic discipline — what's this field of study called?
Historiography is the study of the methods used by historians in developing history as an academic discipline.

Once diagnosed almost exclusively in women as a physical illness in the 19th century, this term for ungovernable emotional excess later became the focus of research by Freud and Charcot — what is this condition called?
Hysteria is a term used to mean ungovernable emotional excess and can refer to a temporary state of mind or emotion.

This English independent scientist invented the electron capture detector, was first to spot CFCs spread through the atmosphere, and proposed that the Earth behaves as one self-regulating system. Who was he?
James Lovelock (26 July 1919 - 26 July 2022) was an English independent scientist, environmentalist and futurist.
Endemic to New Caledonia's mountain forests, this bluish-grey, nearly flightless bird sports bright red legs and unique nasal corns shared by no other bird — what is it?
Kagu (Rhynochetos jubatus) is a crested, long-legged, and bluish-grey bird endemic to the dense mountain forests of New Caledonia.

Amphoteric and unreactive, this post-transition metal reacts with both acids and bases, melts at a low temperature, and tarnishes from shiny to dull gray in air — and three of its isotopes end major nuclear decay chains. Which element is it?
Lead is a chemical element with the symbol Pb (from the Latin plumbum) and atomic number 82.

Featuring a distinctive twin-boom design with a central pod housing the cockpit and guns, this American World War II fighter aircraft also served as a night fighter and long-range escort when fitted with drop tanks — which aircraft?
Lockheed P-38 Lightning is an American single-seat, twin-engined fighter aircraft that was used during World War II.
A sugar alcohol used both as a low-calorie sweetener and as a medication to reduce eye and brain pressure. It's poorly absorbed by the intestines. What's the name of this compound?
Mannitol is a type of sugar alcohol used as a sweetener and medication. It is unclear if use is safe in pregnancy.
Used to treat cancers, autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, and even ectopic pregnancies, this chemotherapy drug and immune suppressant can be taken either orally or by injection — name it?
Methotrexate is a chemotherapy agent and immune-system suppressant.
First documented with ice cream and water by a Tanzanian student and his professor in the 1960s, this contested observation says warmer liquids can outrace colder ones to freezing — what's it called?
Mpemba effect is the observation that very hot liquids or colloids (such as ice cream) can freeze more quickly than colder ones, for similar volumes and surrounding conditions.
Found in tobacco and trace amounts of tomatoes and eggplants, this nightshade alkaloid is used recreationally as a stimulant yet acts as a deadly neurotoxin to insects — what is it?
Nicotine is an alkaloid found primarily in plants of the nightshade family, notably in tobacco; it is also synthesized.
Many species in this cosmopolitan, often-fragrant family live as epiphytes on trees, and some have ditched leaves entirely — relying on highly specialized pollination tricks instead. What are they?
Orchid are plants that belong to the family Orchidaceae, a diverse and widespread group of flowering plants with blooms that are often colourful and fragrant.
This New York Times columnist of 24 years was the sole winner of the 2008 Nobel in economics for explaining the patterns of international trade and where economic activity clusters. Who is he?
Paul Krugman (born February 28, 1953) is an American economist who is the Distinguished Professor of Economics at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York.
With a musty odor like freshly cut hay, this toxic colorless gas is the double acyl-chloride cousin of carbonic acid, and it saw grim use as a chemical weapon in World War I. Name the compound?
Phosgene is an organic chemical compound with the formula COCl2.
Native to cool temperate regions of the Old World, which poplar species is commonly known as European or quaking aspen?
Populus tremula (commonly called aspen, common aspen, Eurasian aspen, European aspen, or quaking aspen) is a species of poplar native to cool temperate regions of the Old World.
Like a cosmic lighthouse, this highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star is only visible from Earth when its beam of radiation sweeps directly toward us — what's the object?
Pulsar (pulsating star, on the model of quasar) is a highly magnetized rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation out of its magnetic poles.
Also called king's crown or Arctic root, this Arctic-growing perennial is widely sold as a supplement even though regulators say its health claims lack solid evidence — which plant?
Rhodiola rosea (commonly golden root, rose root, roseroot, Aaron's rod, Arctic root, king's crown, lignum rhodium, orpin rose) is a perennial flowering plant in the family Crassulaceae.
Having taught economics at the Catholic University of Asunción and once served as Paraguay's finance minister, this politician assumed his country's presidency in 2023 — who is he?
Santiago Peña (Spanish; born 16 November 1978) is a Paraguayan politician and economist who has served as the 52nd president of Paraguay since 2023.
This macrofungus, native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, is now cultivated and consumed around the globe as one of its most widely eaten mushrooms. What mushroom is this?
Shiitake is a macrofungus native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, which is cultivated and consumed around the globe.

This now-discredited scientific theory held that living creatures like fleas or maggots could regularly arise directly from non-living matter such as dust or rotting flesh, and was coherently synthesized by Aristotle. Name the theory?
Spontaneous generation is a superseded scientific theory that held that living creatures could arise from non-living matter and that such processes were commonplace and regular.

This amniote lineage — one of just two major branches alongside the reptile-and-bird clade — is marked by a single temporal opening behind the eye and gave rise to every mammal alive today — name the group?
Synapsida is a diverse group of tetrapod vertebrates that includes all mammals and their extinct relatives.
Writing in 1798, this English cleric-economist warned that abundance only fuels population growth, eventually restoring poverty and hardship for the lower classes — who is he?
Thomas Robert Malthus (13/14 February 1766 - 29 December 1834) was an English economist, cleric, and scholar influential in the fields of political economy and demography.
Egypt and Iraq both flew this Soviet-designed jet bomber in wars against Israel, and China still produces an updated license-built version, the H-6K — which aircraft?
Tupolev Tu-16 (USAF/DOD reporting name Type 39; NATO reporting name: Badger) is a twin-engined jet strategic heavy bomber used by the Soviet Union.
This canid genus contains the 'true foxes' — smaller and bushier-tailed than any wolf or jackal, typically living two to four years, occasionally a decade — which genus?
Vulpes is a genus of the subfamily Caninae.

This Polish-American scholar served as Jimmy Carter's national security advisor from 1977 to 1981 and helped organize an influential international policy group known as the Trilateral Commission — who is he?
Zbigniew Brzezinski (March 28, 1928 - May 26, 2017) was a Polish-American diplomat and political scientist.
This term for cancer that begins in gland cells applies to the most common form of breast cancer and one of the two major types of esophageal cancer — which term?
De Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter
Adenocarcinoma: Cancer of epithelial cells with glandular origin or characteristics.

Often called the greatest mathematician of the twentieth century, this German-born Frenchman revolutionized algebraic geometry before abruptly leaving his post at a Paris research institute in 1970 — who is he?

These coiled-shelled cephalopods, more closely related to octopuses than to nautiluses despite the resemblance, thrived from the Devonian until vanishing around the dinosaur extinction 66 million years ago — what are they?
Ammonoidea: Extinct subclass of cephalopod molluscs.
Known by the symbol Sb and mined chiefly from stibnite ore, which element has long been powdered into the cosmetic kohl and today hardens lead in car batteries?
Antimony: Chemical element with atomic number 51 (Sb)
These chitin-armored invertebrates must shed their exoskeletons to grow and circulate haemolymph through an open body cavity — and may number up to ten million species. What are they?
Arthropod: Phylum of invertebrates with jointed exoskeletons.

Flown by the Royal Air Force's Red Arrows display team, this British jet-powered advanced trainer has been license-built in India by Hindustan Aeronautics, with over 1,000 sold to 18 countries — which aircraft?
BAE Systems Hawk: Military training aircraft family.

This Swiss-American engineer was the only one of a famous physicist's three known biological grandsons to survive childhood, and later earned patents in electronics while working at Texas Instruments — who was he?

Developed to supplement the 727 on short routes, this narrow-body twinjet kept the 707's fuselage width and six-abreast seating and entered service with Lufthansa in 1968 — which best-selling aircraft is it?
A tree-like cluster of dark-green flower heads sprouting from a thick pale stalk, this cabbage-family vegetable is a close cousin of cauliflower and can be eaten raw or cooked — what is it?
Broccoli: Edible green plant in the cabbage family.
Named to honor the Virgin Mary and her golden crown, this daisy-family flower is also known as the pot marigold — which plant?
Calendula officinalis: Species of flowering plant in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Known also as yoke elm, this species of hornbeam native to Western Asia and Europe grows only up to elevations of about 1,000 metres — which species?
Carpinus betulus: Species of tree. It requires a warm climate for good growth, and occurs only at elevations up to 1,000 metres (3,300 ft).
Often called 'the father of the computer,' this English polymath designed the difference engine and the analytical engine, borrowing a punch-card principle from the Jacquard loom — who is he?
Charles Babbage: English mathematician, philosopher, and engineer (1791–1871)
One of the original citrus fruits, this large fragrant relative of the lemon has a thick, coarse rind and is a genetic ancestor of most modern citrus hybrids — what is it?
In mathematics, this is a selection of items from a set where the order of choosing them does not matter, unlike a permutation — what is it called?

Combination: Selection of items from a set. In mathematics, a combination is a selection of items from a set that has distinct members, such that the order of selection does not matter (unlike permutations).
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on where you stand, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Americas — what is it?
Cougar: Wild cat species native to the Americas.
Native to Mexico and Central America, this tuberous flowering plant blooms in nearly every hue except blue, and its tubers store energy as inulin rather than starch — what is it?
Dahlia: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.

Historically defined by having two embryonic seed leaves, this once-standard division of flowering plants covers around 200,000 species but turned out not to share one common ancestor — which plant group?
Dicotyledon: Historical grouping of flowering plants.
One of the very first vertebrate apex predators on Earth, this armor-plated, jointed-neck fish patrolled open Devonian seas some 380 million years ago — which genus?
This Russian economist served as Vladimir Putin's economic adviser before becoming governor of the Central Bank of Russia — who is she?

Elvira Nabiullina: Russian economist and Governor of the Bank of Russia. Elvira Sakhipzadovna Nabiullina (born 29 October 1963) is a Russian economist and current governor of the Central Bank of Russia.
This branch of anthropology studies individual cultures through participant observation, with roots in early 20th-century social science — what is this field called?
Ethnography: Systematic study of people and cultures.
Birds of prey in the genus Falco, some small species are called hobbies and hover-hunters are called kestrels — what are they collectively known as?
Falcon: Birds of prey in the genus Falco. The largest falcon is the gyrfalcon at up to 65 cm (26 in) in length.
Members of the order Siphonaptera, these flightless blood-sucking parasites can leap 50 times their own body length — what are they?
Flea: Insects of the order Siphonaptera. Flea, the common name for the order Siphonaptera, includes 2,500 species of small flightless insects that live as external parasites of mammals and birds.
Found in the rainforests and savannas of sub-Saharan Africa, this snake has the longest fangs of any venomous species — up to two inches — and the highest venom yield of any snake — which snake?
Gaboon viper: Species of snake. It is the largest member of the genus Bitis.
Known only from teeth and four jawbones, this extinct genus of giant ape roamed China for nearly two million years and is now thought to be a close relative of the orangutan — what is it?
Gigantopithecus: Extinct genus of primate. The species may have been sexually dimorphic, with males much bigger than females.

Native from Mexico down to southern Brazil, this large arboreal lizard can grow past six feet long, is a popular but demanding pet, and has become invasive in many warm regions worldwide — which species?
Green iguana: Species of reptile. Usually, this animal is simply called the iguana.

Named after a bird of prey, this British-developed attack aircraft was the only truly successful vertical-takeoff design of its era, able to fly from car parks and forest clearings instead of vulnerable airbases — which aircraft?
Harrier jump jet: Multirole combat aircraft family by Hawker Siddeley, later British Aerospace.

A Greek physician and philosopher of the classical era, this figure is hailed as the "Father of Medicine" for championing prognosis, clinical observation, and the now-discredited theory of bodily humors — who is he?
Hippocrates: Ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE)
Though phylogenetically closer to cats, these African carnivores resemble dogs thanks to convergent evolution, and their family has just four living species — what animal is it?
This probability principle holds that a randomly typing creature, given endless time, would almost surely reproduce the complete works of Shakespeare — what's it called?
Infinite monkey theorem: Counterintuitive result in probability.

A Manhattan Project veteran, this American physicist won a share of the 1975 Nobel Prize for proposing that not all atomic nuclei are spherical — an idea later confirmed by Aage Bohr and Ben Mottelson. Who was he?
James Rainwater: American physicist. Rainwater joined the physics faculty at Columbia in 1946, where he reached the rank of full professor in 1952 and was named Pupin Professor of Physics in 1982.
Dubbed the 'Angel of Death,' this German physician held doctorates in both anthropology and medicine before joining the SS and selecting Auschwitz prisoners for the gas chambers — who was he?
Josef Mengele: Nazi SS doctor at Auschwitz (1911–1979)
Made from shredded pastry dough layered with cheese and soaked in sugar syrup, this Arab dessert is especially popular during Ramadan, with a famous variant hailing from Nablus — what is it?

An Atlanta factory superintendent with a Cornell engineering degree, he was wrongly convicted of murdering a young employee, then kidnapped from prison and lynched — a case that became a focus of antisemitism. Who was he?
Nicknamed "Connie" and instantly recognizable by its triple tail and dolphin-shaped fuselage, which four-engined airliner was the first civil aircraft family to widely use a pressurized cabin?
Lockheed Constellation: Family of US airliners with 4 piston engines, 1943.
This age-related eye disease gradually damages the retina's central region, with a 'wet' form involving leaking blood vessels and a 'dry' form marked by deposits called drusen — what is it?
Macular degeneration: Vision loss due to damage to the macula of the eye.

Endemic to North America and known for long, upward-curving upper tusks with little to no lower tusks, this proboscidean's genus split from other elephant relatives at least 28 million years ago — which ancient beast?
In medicine, this term describes a disease spreading from a primary site to a secondary one — most often used for a cancer seeding new tumors elsewhere in the body — what is it?
Metastasis: Spreading of a disease inside a body. The newly pathological sites, then, are metastases (mets).
Cultivated by the Aztecs and named partly for a Mexican state capital, this flower opens each evening between four and eight o'clock and perfumes the night before closing by morning — which plant?

Mirabilis jalapa: Species of flower. Mirabilis jalapa, the marvel of Peru or four o'clock flower, is the most commonly grown ornamental species of Mirabilis plant, and is available in a range of colors.
Serving as Turkey's minister overseeing environment and climate, who is set to preside over the 2026 UN Climate Change Conference, COP31?
A healthy kidney contains up to 1.5 million of these microscopic filtering units, each pairing a capillary tuft with a cup-shaped capsule — what is it called?
Nephron: Microscopic structural and functional unit of the kidney.
The largest structure inside a eukaryotic cell's nucleus, this site of ribosome assembly also helps form signal recognition particles and responds to cellular stress — what is it?
Nucleolus: Largest structure in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. The nucleolus also participates in the formation of signal recognition particles and plays a role in the cell's response to stress.

This vertebrate clade has skeletons made mostly of bone rather than cartilage, and includes both classic 'bony fish' and, cladistically, every land vertebrate descended from lobe-finned ancestors — what is it?
Osteichthyes: Diverse clade of vertebrate animals.
Named from the Latin word for 'sparrow,' this bird order — making up over half of all species — is defined by perching feet with three toes forward and one back. What's it called?
Passerine: Perching birds of the order Passeriformes.
This Belgian-British microbiologist helped discover the Ebola virus in 1976, fought to contain its first recorded outbreak, then became a pioneering AIDS researcher — who is he?
Known as the Scots pine in Britain, this Eurasian conifer is identifiable by its blue-green needles and orange-red bark — which species?
Pinus sylvestris: Species of conifer. Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Also known as niter or saltpeter, this compound is a key ingredient of traditional gunpowder and gives cured meats their reddish color — what is it?
Potassium nitrate: Chemical compound. Potassium nitrate is a chemical compound with a sharp, salty, bitter taste and the chemical formula KNO3.
Fossils of this genus, found in Germany's Solnhofen limestone, mark the first pterosaur ever identified as a flying reptile — which genus?
Pterodactylus: Genus of pterodactyloid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic.
Belonging to the genus Corvus and distinguished from its close relatives mainly by size, the largest species in this bird category are also the largest of all perching birds — which bird?
Raven: Index of animals with the same common name.
This Israeli-American mathematician shared the 2005 Nobel in Economics with Thomas Schelling for illuminating conflict and cooperation through game theory — who is he?
Caused by bacteria in the Salmonella genus, this common form of food poisoning brings diarrhea, fever, and cramps within 12 to 36 hours of eating contaminated food — what is it called?
Salmonellosis: Infection caused by Salmonella bacteria. It is one of the most common diseases to be known as food poisoning (though the name refers to food-borne illness in general).

Caused by a sudden burst of synchronized electrical activity in the brain, this neurological event affects roughly 50 million people worldwide and can range from a brief blank stare to a full convulsion — what is it?
Seizure: Period of symptoms due to excessive or synchronous neuronal brain activity.
This structural framework supporting an animal's body can take the form of a rigid outer shell, an internal bony frame, or simply fluid pressure inside the body. What is it?
Skeleton: Part of the body that forms the supporting structure.

Encased by the vertebral column and running from the brainstem down to about the first lumbar vertebra, this hollow, fluid-filled structure forms the other half of the central nervous system alongside the brain — what is it?
Spinal cord: Part of the vertebral column in animals.

Native to New Guinea and domesticated by Papuan and Austronesian peoples, this tall grass with sucrose-rich stalks was carried across the Pacific and eventually to India and China in ancient times. What crop is it?
Sugarcane: Several species of grass used for sugar production.
